power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Models based on administrative population health records can help improve understanding of disease and hospitalisation risk.
This understanding can support evidence-based population health policy and processes.
Influenza and other acute respiratory diseases place a large, inequitable burden on the New Zealand population and health care resources.

We have developed and evaluated such models using retrospective New Zealand hospitalisation records linked to other administrative data to estimate individual-level risk of hospitalisation due to acute respiratory infection.
We analysed linked annual records for approximately 4•85-5•36 million people in 2017-2024.
Six machine learning algorithms and eight variable sets were assessed using five-fold cross-validation grouped by demographic profile.
Variables comprised demographics, continuous hospital-based (M3) and pharmaceuticalbased (P3) morbidity indices, and influenza vaccination status.
Models trained on one year were also evaluated on data from the following year.
Performance measures were the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the average precision score (APS).
SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) described model contributions, including paired vaccination-input changes in 2024.
Findings: Annual national hospitalisation prevalence ranged from 1•01% to 1•60%.
With all variables, mean cross-validation AUROC and APS were 0•8430 and 0•1283 for LightGBM (LGB), and 0•8415 and 0•1285 for XGBoost (XGB).
Adding both morbidity indices to the demographics increased LGB APS from 0•0720 to 0•1158; adding vaccination further increased it to 0•1283.
Next-year AUROC and APS averaged 0•8429 and 0•1267 for LGB and 0•8423 and 0•1277 for XGB.
Age and morbidity were the most influential variables.
Among vaccinated individuals, SHAP analysis indicated that vaccination contributed most strongly towards lower modelestimated hospitalisation risk in the oldest age group.

Interpretation: Combining historical morbidity and vaccination information in gradient boosting models improved the ability to distinguish between people who experienced respiratory hospitalisation and those who did not in annual New Zealand population data.

Similar next-year performance and interpretable variation across age and morbidity profiles support further development toward practical risk assessment, including calibration and evaluation across population groups.

Evidence before this study Our focused narrative review considered population-based respiratory hospitalisation models, respiratory disease burden in New Zealand, and the development of the M3 and P3 morbidity indices.

Existing studies include population models for COVID-19 and infant respiratory syncytial virus, risk-factor analyses of broad respiratory admissions, and evidence that hospital and pharmaceutical morbidity measures provide complementary information.

This is the first evaluation of national hospitalisation data linked to other national administrative data to model the risk of acute respiratory infection admission across eight annual datasets, comparing six algorithms and eight variable sets.

Together with the benchmark results, these findings illustrate how gradient boosting applied to population-scale records can represent and explain combinations of routinely recorded health information.
Quantifying historical morbidity and including vaccination information improved respiratory hospitalisation classification, with gradient boosting providing the strongest overall performance.
The explanatory analyses further showed that vaccination-related contributions depended on the individual's age and morbidity profile.

Representing these clinically plausible patterns supports the use of flexible, non-linear models, such as tree-based algorithms, and rich population-scale records for developing interpretable respiratory risk assessments.
The study establishes a basis for a New Zealand respiratory risk model by identifying effective algorithms and useful combinations of variables.
Respiratory infections are a substantial cause of hospitalisation, and their burden is unevenly distributed across the population.
New Zealand studies have documented inequalities in serious infectious disease admissions and respiratory hospitalisation burden associated with age, ethnicity, and deprivation 1, 2 .
text.formatted: New Zealand studies have documented inequalities in serious infectious disease admissions and respiratory hospitalisation burden associated with age, ethnicity, and deprivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Identifying people at greater risk could support prevention and guided discussions between patients and general practitioners about modifiable risk factors and mitigation strategies.

Routinely collected population records allow us to investigate this vulnerability across a broad range of respiratory hospitalisation outcomes without requiring new clinical measurements and participant burden.
Many respiratory models concern outcomes after infection or presentation to healthcare 3, 4 .
text.formatted: Many respiratory models concern outcomes after infection or presentation to healthcare <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> .

text.text: Population-based examples include QCOVID for COVID-19 hospitalisation and mortality among adults, and a registry-based model of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalisation among infants 5, 6 .
text.formatted: Population-based examples include QCOVID for COVID-19 hospitalisation and mortality among adults, and a registry-based model of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalisation among infants <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: A Scottish national study also identified age, deprivation, existing conditions, and previous admissions as risk factors for a broad group of acute respiratory infection admissions 7 .
text.formatted: A Scottish national study also identified age, deprivation, existing conditions, and previous admissions as risk factors for a broad group of acute respiratory infection admissions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: While forecasting aggregate respiratory admissions to predict healthcare demand in New Zealand has been addressed 8 , an individual-level model to identify people at increased risk of hospitalisation is lacking.
text.formatted: While forecasting aggregate respiratory admissions to predict healthcare demand in New Zealand has been addressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> , an individual-level model to identify people at increased risk of hospitalisation is lacking.

text.text: An individual model can help discern baseline risk due to unmodifiable characteristics, such as age, from modifiable factors and identify relative contributions of different factors to overall risk.

The integration of variables was informed by international literature on risk factors for severe influenza, which highlights age and underlying health conditions as important determinants of severe outcomes 9 .
Representing the combined burden of long-term conditions is therefore an important consideration in developing an individual risk model.

In New Zealand, the Measuring Multimorbidity (M3) and Pharmaceutical Prescribing Profile (P3) indices summarise historical morbidity using hospital diagnoses and pharmaceutical dispensing, respectively 10, 11 .
text.formatted: In New Zealand, the Measuring Multimorbidity (M3) and Pharmaceutical Prescribing Profile (P3) indices summarise historical morbidity using hospital diagnoses and pharmaceutical dispensing, respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: These indices offer a practical way to incorporate information about multiple conditions from routinely collected records and to assess whether the two sources provide complementary information.

Influenza vaccination is also relevant as an established preventive measure against an important cause of respiratory hospitalisation and, unlike age and most medical conditions, represents a modifiable factor 12 .
text.formatted: Influenza vaccination is also relevant as an established preventive measure against an important cause of respiratory hospitalisation and, unlike age and most medical conditions, represents a modifiable factor <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Together with demographic and deprivation variables, these measures provide a starting point for establishing a population model using routinely available information.
Investigating the contribution of these variables provides a foundation for subsequent models incorporating more detailed clinical, behavioural, and environmental variables.
Using New Zealand population data, we aimed to develop and evaluate a model that distinguishes between people with and without a hospital admission for respiratory infectious disease.

Using linked annual population records from 2017 to 2024, we compared modelling approaches and quantified the extent to which models improved by incorporating historical morbidity and influenza vaccination data, in addition to demographic variables.
We also examined whether models maintained their performance when applied to the following year and explored how age, morbidity, and vaccination contributed to model estimates.

We conducted a retrospective population-level classification study using linked records from the Stats NZ Integrated Data Infrastructure (IDI), a secure research database linking de-identified administrative and survey records about people and households in New Zealand.
Annual datasets covered 2017-2024.
Sources included population and address records aggregated to the mesh block level, hospital discharge information, immunisation records, and pharmaceutical dispensing records.
The unit of analysis was the person within an annual dataset; individuals could appear in several years.
People with missing required information were excluded before modelling, and no imputation was applied.

The binary outcome indicated at least one qualifying hospitalisation during the calendar year, identified using a broad set of respiratory disease codes from the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision, Australian Modification (ICD-10-AM).
The complete code list is provided in Table S1 (supplementary material).
text.formatted: The complete code list is provided in Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> (supplementary material).

text.text: Codes were selected to achieve some specificity for influenza and based on previous literature 1, 13 , clinical advice and codes most commonly associated with influenza-positive SARI cases from the SHIVERS study 14.
text.formatted: Codes were selected to achieve some specificity for influenza and based on previous literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> , clinical advice and codes most commonly associated with influenza-positive SARI cases from the SHIVERS study <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: Demographics comprised age, sex, and area-level deprivation score 15 and five non-exclusive ethnicity indicators: Asian, European, Māori, Pacific peoples, and Middle Eastern, Latin American, and African (MELAA).
text.formatted: Demographics comprised age, sex, and area-level deprivation score <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> and five non-exclusive ethnicity indicators: Asian, European, Māori, Pacific peoples, and Middle Eastern, Latin American, and African (MELAA).

text.text: Individuals could identify with more than one ethnic group.
All five binary ethnicity variables were retained simultaneously, giving eight demographic input columns.

In tables and plots, Europe and Pacific denote European and Pacific peoples, respectively; DEP denotes the deprivation score, FV denotes the influenza vaccination status, and Demo denotes the demographic variable set.
To incorporate information on individual multimorbidity, we used the M3 and P3 indices, developed by Stanley and colleagues using New Zealand population health data 10, 11 .
text.formatted: To incorporate information on individual multimorbidity, we used the M3 and P3 indices, developed by Stanley and colleagues using New Zealand population health data <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: M3 and P3 indices were derived from linked IDI records and included as continuous variables.
M3 used hospital diagnoses from the five years before each annual snapshot, whereas P3 used pharmaceutical dispensing records from the preceding year.
Neither index included information from the outcome year.
For hospitalised individuals, FV was one (FV=1) if vaccination occurred in the same calendar year at least 14 days before the qualifying admission.
For people without hospitalisation, FV was one if vaccination occurred at any time during that year; otherwise, it was zero (FV=0).

Eight variable sets were evaluated: demographics alone; demographics with FV, M3, or P3 separately; demographics with M3 and P3; demographics with FV and either morbidity index; and demographics with all three.
The full set contained 11 input columns.
Table 1 summarises the characteristics of the 2024 study population overall and by hospitalisation status.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> summarises the characteristics of the 2024 study population overall and by hospitalisation status.

text.text: We treated hospitalisation as a binary classification task: each annual record was labelled as having at least one qualifying hospital admission (1) or not (0).
During training, machine learning classification algorithms learned relationships between the recorded variables and these labels.
Each fitted model then produced a continuous score between 0 and 1 for the hospitalisation class, with higher scores indicating greater model-estimated hospitalisation risk.
We evaluated how well these scores distinguished people with and without hospitalisation, without selecting a threshold to assign individuals to either class.
We used scores from the class-balanced models to rank individuals by hospitalisation risk and did not assess calibration.
We compared logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), LightGBM (LGB), XGBoost (XGB), and single-tree versions of LightGBM and XGBoost, labelled Tree (lgb) and Tree (xgb) [16] [17] [18] .
text.formatted: We compared logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), LightGBM (LGB), XGBoost (XGB), and single-tree versions of LightGBM and XGBoost, labelled Tree (lgb) and Tree (xgb) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> .

text.text: RF combines the outputs of multiple decision trees, whereas LGB and XGB build trees sequentially, with each additional tree refining the combined model.
The ensembles used 100 trees (the default parameter), and the single-tree versions used 1 boosting iteration.
LR included linear terms for continuous variables on the log-odds scale and no interaction terms, serving as a linear baseline model.
Decision-tree models can accommodate nonlinear relationships and interactions without specifying these patterns in advance.
Analyses were conducted on the raw individual-level data in secure Stats NZ Data Labs.
Computational constraints in the Data Lab informed the choice of algorithms and fixed settings; no hyperparameter tuning was performed (see supplementary material Table S2).
text.formatted: Computational constraints in the Data Lab informed the choice of algorithms and fixed settings; no hyperparameter tuning was performed (see supplementary material Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Five non-overlapping test folds were formed within each year using demographic-profile groups.
A profile combined age band, sex, the five ethnicity indicators, and a 10-step deprivation band.
One representative was randomly selected from each profile, and a five-fold stratified allocation was applied to these representatives based on their outcomes.
All individuals with a given profile were assigned to the same fold.
Each fold was held out once, with approximately 80% of annual records used for training and 20% for testing.

This profile grouping was applied to ensure that multiple samples with the same or very similar combinations of variable values are represented in both the training and testing sets, which can be an issue for the model when using only demographic variables, as these are mainly categorical.
The same folds were used across algorithms and variable sets within the cross-validation.
Variables were standardised using means and standard deviations fitted to each training set, then transformed in the held-out data.
Class balancing was applied during training, using the appropriate algorithm parameters.
LR used balanced class weights; XGB used the negative-to-positive training count ratio; LGB used its classimbalance option; and RF used corresponding observation weights.
Hospitalisation caused by respiratory infection, whilst making a large contribution to seasonal hospital admissions, is infrequent at the population level.
In the annual datasets, approximately 1•5% to 1•6% of people had a qualifying admission in most years (Table 2).
text.formatted: In the annual datasets, approximately 1•5% to 1•6% of people had a qualifying admission in most years (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Most people do not have a hospital admission.
This is termed a class imbalance, which makes overall classification accuracy uninformative on its own.
For example, a naïve model that always predicts no hospitalisation achieves an accuracy of 98•5% at a prevalence of 1•5%.

Therefore, we use threshold-independent performance measures to evaluate model performance and focus on the average precision score (APS), as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) can be misleading when class imbalance is high 19.
text.formatted: Therefore, we use threshold-independent performance measures to evaluate model performance and focus on the average precision score (APS), as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) can be misleading when class imbalance is high <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref>.

text.text: Fold scores were averaged within each year, and annual means were weighted equally.
These summaries average evaluation scores rather than pooling individual model outputs.
The algorithms were first compared using the full variable set; variable-set comparisons then focused on LGB and XGB.
Increments from adding FV were matched by year and fold against the corresponding set without FV.
For next-year evaluation, models trained on complete annual datasets from 2017 through 2023 were applied to the following year's population.
Training-year transformations and class weights were retained.
Scores were averaged equally across seven year-pairs and compared with cross-validation results for the same evaluation years.
This assesses temporal transfer within the national data system, where individuals can overlap between years.
Overall performance summaries included all eight cross-validation years (2017-2024) and all seven next-year evaluations (supplementary Tables S3-S6).

text.text: Values were normalised separately within each fitted model and importance type, then averaged across folds and years and expressed as percentages.
SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) describe how each variable contributes to an individual model-estimated hospitalisation risk.
All variable contributions, together with a model-specific reference value, sum to the model estimate (on the log-odds scale) 20 .
text.formatted: All variable contributions, together with a model-specific reference value, sum to the model estimate (on the log-odds scale) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: For this analysis, the original models and real records inside the Data Lab were used.
SHAP values were derived for a subset of 1,000,000 people randomly selected from the full dataset for the same year or the next year.
A subset was used to reduce computational resource requirements.
Based on the small variation observed in model performance across cross-validation folds, we expect that a random subset covering ~20% of the data reflects the distributions of the full dataset.
To visualise the SHAP analyses of the models, we used beeswarm plots (Figure 5 and Supplementary Figure S1).
text.formatted: To visualise the SHAP analyses of the models, we used beeswarm plots (Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> and Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref>).

text.text: These allowed us to examine the magnitude and direction of variable contributions on the log-odds scale.
Note that we selected LGB for the SHAP analysis, as this is the model for which we, together with Stats NZ, found a reliable workflow to release trained models after confidentiality processing.
Besides XGB, LGB achieved the highest model performance scores.
We used TreeExplainer, an efficient implementation for deriving SHAP values from tree-based models 20.
text.formatted: We used TreeExplainer, an efficient implementation for deriving SHAP values from tree-based models <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref>.

text.text: Among people with observed FV=1 in 2024, we conducted a descriptive paired analysis using the full-variable LGB model fitted to the complete 2024 analysis dataset.
Each individual was evaluated twice with TreeExplainer, with FV set to one and zero, holding all other variables, the fitted model, and explainer settings fixed.
Differences were defined as SHAP with FV=1 minus SHAP with FV=0.
Negative values indicate lower contributions under FV=1.
We summarised FV and age differences by medians and quartiles within five age groups, labelled 0-1, 1-5, 5-15, 15-65, and 65+, overall and separately for M3=P3=0 and M3 ≠ 0 or P3 ≠ 0.
Both indices remained continuous model variables.
This analysis describes the fitted model's response in the training records and does not estimate causal effects of vaccination.
Annual analysis populations ranged from 4,851,537 in 2017 to 5,355,516 in 2024 (Table 2).
text.formatted: Annual analysis populations ranged from 4,851,537 in 2017 to 5,355,516 in 2024 (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Between 51,057 and 85,575 people had a qualifying hospitalisation each year.
Prevalence was 1•51-1•60% in 2017-2019 and 2022-2024, compared with 1•01% in 2020 and 1•19% in 2021.
Characteristics of the 2024 analysis population are presented overall and by respiratory hospitalisation status in Table 1.
text.formatted: Characteristics of the 2024 analysis population are presented overall and by respiratory hospitalisation status in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Compared with individuals without qualifying hospitalisation, hospitalised individuals were more frequently aged 65 years or older (39•4 % versus 16•8 %) and belonged to the highest deprivation quintile (29•2 % versus 20•5 %).
A greater proportion also had M3 > 0 (41•7 % versus 11•5 %) or P3 > 0 (66•7 % versus 42•5 %).
text.formatted: A greater proportion also had M3 > 0 (41•7 % versus 11•5 %) or P3 > 0 (66•7 % versus 42•5 %).

text.text: LGB and XGB had the strongest average performance with the full set of variables (Figure 1; supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: LGB and XGB had the strongest average performance with the full set of variables (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1;</ref> supplementary Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: LGB achieved mean AUROC 0 The APS achieved by LGB was highest in 2019 (0•1394) and lowest in 2020 (0•1067), whereas its highest AUROC occurred in 2021 (0•8624).
XGB showed the same pattern, with corresponding values of 0•1395, 0•1056, and 0•8603.
Comparing 2017-2019 with 2022-2024, mean LGB APS was 0•1357 versus 0•1291, and AUROC was 0•8411 versus 0•8367.
XGB showed similar period differences.
Mean hospitalisation prevalence was almost unchanged (1•568% vs 1•562%).
Both morbidity indices improved performance across all years (Figure 2 and supplementary material Tables S4 and S5).
text.formatted: Both morbidity indices improved performance across all years (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">2</ref> and supplementary material Tables <ref type="table">S4</ref> and <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: For LGB, demographics alone yielded an AUROC of 0•7856 and an APS of 0•0720.
Adding M3 increased these to 0•8259 and 0•1034; adding P3 increased them to 0•8297 and 0•0998.
Including both indices yielded an AUROC of 0•8400 and an APS of 0•1158.
XGB followed the same pattern: AUROC increased from 0•7830 to 0•8382 and APS from 0•0713 to 0•1154 with both indices.
Relative APS increases were 60•8% for LGB and 61•9% for XGB.
The added value of FV depended on the other variables.
For LGB, FV increased APS by 0•0054 with demographics alone and by 0•0124 when both indices were included.
XGB increments were 0•0055 and 0•0131, respectively.
Gains with either index separately were intermediate (Table S6, see supplementary material).
text.formatted: Gains with either index separately were intermediate (Table <ref type="table">S6</ref>, see supplementary material).

text.text: Age, M3, and P3 accounted for 96•2% of LGB gain and 90•4% of XGB gain with all variables (Figure 3;  supplementary Table S7).
text.formatted: Age, M3, and P3 accounted for 96•2% of LGB gain and 90•4% of XGB gain with all variables (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">3;</ref>  supplementary Table <ref type="table">S7</ref>).

text.text: Their mean LGB gain shares were 44•69%, 36•58%, and 14•91%, respectively.
Age contributed the largest share in seven years; M3 ranked first in 2020.
P3 ranked third in every annual LGB gain summary.
Deprivation accounted for 15•98% of LGB splits and 24•15% of XGB splits, compared with gain shares of 1•45% and 3•74%.
FV accounted for 1•12% of LGB gain and 3•14% of splits.
Next-year AUROC and APS averaged 0•8429 and 0•1267 for LGB and 0•8423 and 0•1277 for XGB.
Aligned to the same evaluation years, mean next-year minus cross-validation differences were -0•0007 for AUROC and -0•0009 for APS for LGB, and +0•0003 and -0•0001 for XGB (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Aligned to the same evaluation years, mean next-year minus cross-validation differences were -0•0007 for AUROC and -0•0009 for APS for LGB, and +0•0003 and -0•0001 for XGB (Figure <ref type="figure">4</ref>).

text.text: Improvements from morbidity and FV remained apparent in next-year evaluations (supplementary Tables S3-S6).
text.formatted: Improvements from morbidity and FV remained apparent in next-year evaluations (supplementary Tables <ref type="table">S3-S6</ref>).

text.text: Across the beeswarm plots, age, P3, and M3 occupied the first three displayed positions.
Both young and older ages were among the positive contributions, as expected.
Higher morbidity indices and deprivation generally contributed positively, whereas recorded vaccination generally contributed negatively.
Figure 5 compares nextyear and same-year explanations for 2018 and 2024 (see supplementary material, Figure S1, for profiles derived from other years).
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> compares nextyear and same-year explanations for 2018 and 2024 (see supplementary material, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S1</ref>, for profiles derived from other years).

text.text: Broad patterns were similar, although the ordering and contributions of some variables varied.
Setting FV to one produced a negative median change in the FV contribution across all displayed age groups (Figure 6).
text.formatted: Setting FV to one produced a negative median change in the FV contribution across all displayed age groups (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">6</ref>).

text.text: Among all vaccinated individuals within each group, median changes ranged from -0•327 to -0•418 in the four younger groups and reached -0•656 in the 65+ group.
Median age-contribution changes were close to zero in younger groups (-0•001 to 0•029), compared with -0•171 in the 65+ group.

Within that oldest group, changes were more negative when either morbidity index was nonzero than when both were zero: median FV changes were -0•675 versus -0•527, and age changes were -0•177 versus -0•145.
All differences are in modeloutput units, not in model-estimated probability.

Using linked New Zealand population records, we compared classification algorithms and quantified the extent to which historical morbidity and influenza vaccination information improved the ability to distinguish people with and without respiratory hospitalisation.
Integrating hospital-and pharmaceutical-based morbidity indices improves models.
Furthermore, our results show that these indices are complementary, with the highest APS achieved when models incorporate both.
Additionally, recorded influenza vaccination provided a further improvement, with the greatest effect when both morbidity indices were included.
With all variables included, Tree (xgb) achieved a higher mean APS than RF (0•1054 vs 0•0720) despite a similar mean AUROC (0•8244 vs 0•8240).
While the YDF random forest always uses a random subset of variables at each split, potentially omitting the important ones, the single XGB tree could consider all variables at every split.
This difference may partly explain the single tree's higher APS, while successive trees in the XGB and LGB ensembles could further refine the ranking of people at elevated risk.
The paired vaccination analysis showed how gradient boosting captured clinically plausible joint patterns in our data.
For each vaccinated person in the 2024 analysis, we changed only the vaccination input.

Recording vaccination as present produced the largest median downward shifts in both the vaccination and age contributions among people aged 65 years and older, particularly those with a nonzero morbidity index (at least one medical condition was present).
Even though a person's age is not changed in this analysis, the model assigns different contributions to the age variable based on vaccination status.

This age-morbidity pattern is consistent with the priority given to older adults and people with chronic conditions in influenza vaccination recommendations. 12 Studies of vaccine effectiveness also document variation by age and, among older adults, by condition. 21, 22 The SHAP changes quantify how the fitted model used vaccination information.
text.formatted: This age-morbidity pattern is consistent with the priority given to older adults and people with chronic conditions in influenza vaccination recommendations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> Studies of vaccine effectiveness also document variation by age and, among older adults, by condition. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> The SHAP changes quantify how the fitted model used vaccination information.

text.text: However, estimating vaccine effectiveness within these groups requires a causal analysis.
Age and morbidity helped identify groups vulnerable to severe respiratory illness, but exposure to infection also matters.
Many people with increased estimated risk had no admissions in any of the datasets.
As people with admissions made up only a small fraction of the population, even a low false-positive rate could produce many false positives relative to true positives.
This reduces precision and helps explain why a model can achieve good AUROC alongside modest APS. 19 Accordingly, in 2020, APS fell as the prevalence of qualifying admissions dropped to 1•01%.
text.formatted: This reduces precision and helps explain why a model can achieve good AUROC alongside modest APS. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> Accordingly, in 2020, APS fell as the prevalence of qualifying admissions dropped to 1•01%.

text.text: Lockdowns, border restrictions and physical distancing curtailed transmission, 23 and surveillance documented changes in the circulation of influenza and RSV during 2020 and 2021. 24, 25 People vulnerable because of age or chronic illness may have had fewer opportunities to become infected.
text.formatted: Lockdowns, border restrictions and physical distancing curtailed transmission, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> and surveillance documented changes in the circulation of influenza and RSV during 2020 and 2021. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> People vulnerable because of age or chronic illness may have had fewer opportunities to become infected.

text.text: Lower prevalence itself also reduces precision at a given sensitivity and false-positive rate.
The proportion with a qualifying admission rose from 1•19% in 2021 to 1•51% in 2022.

During New Zealand's Omicron waves in 2022, older adults had higher COVID-19 hospitalisation rates. 26 Our study may have included some of these admissions through a qualifying respiratory diagnosis such as viral pneumonia.
text.formatted: During New Zealand's Omicron waves in 2022, older adults had higher COVID-19 hospitalisation rates. <ref type="bibr">26</ref> Our study may have included some of these admissions through a qualifying respiratory diagnosis such as viral pneumonia.

text.text: This suggests some overlap in vulnerability across infections, although the combined outcome prevents us from attributing the rebound to a particular virus.
Compared to the pre-pandemic era, the mean APS achieved by gradient boosting was slightly lower in 2022-2024, despite similar hospitalisation prevalence.

Auckland surveillance documented changes in influenza admission rates and the age profile of admitted adults after restrictions eased, with a different pattern for human metapneumovirus. 2 Changes in circulating pathogens and affected populations may therefore have influenced classification, even when models were refitted each year.
text.formatted: Auckland surveillance documented changes in influenza admission rates and the age profile of admitted adults after restrictions eased, with a different pattern for human metapneumovirus. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> Changes in circulating pathogens and affected populations may therefore have influenced classification, even when models were refitted each year.

text.text: Similar average performance in next-year evaluations supports annual model updates, accompanied by regular assessment as respiratory disease patterns change.
Further development could use linked survey and census records to assess whether information on smoking, household crowding and employment improves classification.
This is worth testing because APS remained well below its maximum of 1•0, which indicates that many variables are missing that could help a model to capture the high-risk group more precisely.
To make the models easier to use during consultations, we could replace M3 and P3 with a short list of conditions that clinicians can readily identify.
Evaluating models based on individual medical conditions rather than the morbidity indices would show whether this can be done without decreasing performance.
However, before the model can support individual health advice, calibration should establish how closely its scores agree with observed hospitalisation rates, with recalibration where needed.

This is particularly relevant given the low prevalence rates. 27 Calibration, sensitivity and positive predictive value at clinically relevant thresholds should be assessed across age, ethnicity and deprivation groups, including Māori and Pacific peoples.
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant given the low prevalence rates. <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27</ref> Calibration, sensitivity and positive predictive value at clinically relevant thresholds should be assessed across age, ethnicity and deprivation groups, including Māori and Pacific peoples.

text.text: Comparisons with models trained within these groups could show whether more specialised models add value.
Clinicians and patients could then assess whether individual explanations support informed discussions about respiratory risk and prevention.
